title: Mirabel and the Well
premise: Ada Crane returns to the family homestead to bury his twin sister Mirabel, only to find the body in the casket wearing his face and the village insisting Mirabel died years ago at the old well. A documentarian by compulsion, Ada records everything—diaries, interviews, and now his own sleep, where a second voice answers questions he never asked aloud. The recordings reveal the truth: the Crane family has traded one twin per generation to the well since 1890, and the count comes due on the night of the funeral wake. To save what remains of his family, Ada must offer the well something it has never been given—the complete record of every debt it has collected—and walk into the water himself as both payment and witness.
about_author: F. M. Okafor is a former archivist from Enugu who spent a decade cataloguing colonial-era estate records before turning to fiction. Their stories explore what families preserve, and what preserves itself inside families.

chapters.title: The Wrong Face
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. Arriving home for the burial, Ada lifts the casket lid and finds his own face staring back. The undertaker insists it's Mirabel; the death certificate bears Ada's name. He begins documenting the discrepancies in a leather notebook, a habit inherited from their mother. Emotional beat: uncanny dread sharpened by grief he cannot locate.

chapters.title: What the Village Remembers
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. Interviews with neighbors yield impossible testimony: Mirabel drowned at the well in 1998, they say, showing him a weathered grave. His aunt Ngozi begs him to stop asking questions and burn the notebook. Ada records her warning instead. Emotional beat: isolation deepening as loyalty to family collides with the need for truth.

chapters.title: Mother's Ledger
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. Searching the attic, Ada finds his mother's hidden ledgers—decades of entries counting days, names, and payments to 'the keeper below.' The final page lists two names: Mirabel, crossed out, and his own, dated the night after the wake. Emotional beat: inheritance revealed as predation.

chapters.title: First Recording
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. Plagued by exhaustion, Ada sets a recorder beside his bed. At 3:11 a.m., a voice—not his—answers questions he hasn't asked, describing the well's interior in loving detail. Playback confirms it. Emotional beat: terror curdling into obsessive fascination; documentation becomes communion.

chapters.title: Ngozi's Confession
chapters.summary: Alternating POV between Ada and Aunt Ngozi. Ngozi admits she was the twin spared in 1972; her brother went down willingly so she could live. She explains the count: the well takes one twin each generation, but it must be offered, not taken. Emotional beat: guilt passed down like property.

chapters.title: Mirabel's Room
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. Ada breaks into the sealed room that was supposedly Mirabel's and finds it untouched since childhood—except fresh flowers and a diary written in his own handwriting, dated into next week. The last entry describes the wake, the fire, and someone screaming his name. Emotional beat: time folding; the future already recorded.

chapters.title: The Count Begins
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs. On the eve of the wake, relatives arrive from across the country, and each nightfall the well's sound carries farther—water where there is no water. The youngest twins in the family, ten-year-old cousins, begin sleepwalking toward the paddock. Ada realizes the well will take them if no adult offers first. Emotional beat: rising dread; the deadline made flesh.

chapters.title: Questions Answered
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. In a final sleep session, Ada asks the second voice directly who he is. The answer: the brother Ngozi lost, still keeping count, still waiting—and willing to tell Ada exactly how an offering works, because he wants to be replaced. Emotional beat: seduction of despair; the dead recruiting the living.

chapters.title: The Wake
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs. The wake erupts when the cousins reach the well; Ngozi throws herself across the mouth of it and is nearly taken. Ada plays his recordings aloud—the full ledger, every name, every debt—forcing the family to hear the truth they've paid to bury. The well goes silent, listening. Emotional beat: climax; truth as weapon and wound.

chapters.title: A Complete Record
chapters.summary: Ada's POV, then epilogue via Ngozi. At dawn Ada walks to the well carrying every document—the ledger, the diaries, the tapes—and offers the well its own history instead of another twin, stepping in as witness rather than victim. The water takes the records and releases the count. Epilogue: the cousins wake remembering nothing; Ngozi finds Ada's notebook on the porch, one new entry in his hand: 'Paid in full.' Emotional beat: sacrifice transmuted into testimony; ambiguous, haunted peace.
